summary: Technology Hardware, Storage and Peripherals is splitting in two. Consumer devices are being squeezed by memory costs: IDC data show third-quarter smartphone shipments down 22% and PC shipments down 20% [2][3]. Infrastructure is booming: Dell holds a $95 billion AI server backlog [4], while Seagate and Western Digital earn operating margins near 50% [6][7]. Apple is the large exception, with record September-quarter revenue of $114.5 billion [1]. Memory pricing is the swing factor for both sides [8]. Sub-industry consensus and current sector multiples were not available to us, so valuation views here rest on single-name data [10][11].

watch: Whether memory prices keep rising: DRAM hit a record in October while NAND stalled after 21 months of increases [8].
IDC warns the worst is yet to come for smartphones and that weak demand could build inventory into 2027 [3].
IDC says a weaker economy could cut PC demand further into 2027, with channel promotions possible [2].
Dell's ability to convert its $95 billion AI server backlog, with supply availability the stated constraint [4].
Whether tariff refunds that flattered Apple and HP margins recur; they are one-off benefits [1][5].

basics.intro: These companies make the physical computers and the devices attached to them: smartphones, PCs, servers, data storage, and printers. Most design the product, buy chips and other parts from suppliers, and pay contract manufacturers in Asia to assemble it. They sell through phone carriers, retailers and resellers, or straight to businesses and cloud companies. Apple is by far the largest company here and also earns a large share of its profit from services sold to iPhone users. Networking gear and the parts inside devices sit in neighbouring sub-industries.

products.name: Smartphones, tablets and wearables
products.what: Consumer devices bought every few years, plus watches and earbuds sold alongside them.
products.examples: Apple iPhone, iPad, Apple Watch and AirPods

products.name: PCs and workstations
products.what: Laptops and desktops for consumers and businesses. Business buyers replace them on regular cycles, often triggered by a new version of Windows.
products.examples: Dell, HP Inc and Lenovo laptops and desktops, Apple Mac

products.name: Servers, including AI servers
products.what: The computers that fill data centres. AI servers pack in several GPUs, cost far more per unit and earn thinner margins than ordinary servers.
products.examples: Dell PowerEdge, Super Micro, Hewlett Packard Enterprise

products.name: Hard disk drives
products.what: Magnetic drives that store large amounts of data cheaply. High-capacity 'nearline' drives sold to cloud data centres are now the main market.

products.name: Flash storage and storage systems
products.what: Solid-state drives, and storage arrays that let a company manage its data across many drives.

products.name: Printers and supplies
products.what: Printers sold at a thin margin, followed by years of profitable ink and toner sales.

products.name: Services built on devices
products.what: App stores, cloud storage, subscriptions, warranties and payment services sold to people who already own the device.

terms.meaning: The number of devices sold into the market in a period, usually counted by research firms such as IDC. They are the headline demand measure for phones and PCs.
Revenue divided by units. A shift towards premium models can lift revenue even when unit sales fall.
The number of devices in use. It drives replacement demand and, for Apple, services revenue.
How many years people and companies keep a device before replacing it. A longer cycle cuts annual demand even if the installed base is stable.
The cost of all the parts in a device. Memory and processors are the largest items, so chip prices feed straight into hardware makers' margins.
A company, often in Taiwan or China, that assembles devices for the brand, such as Foxconn. An ODM (original design manufacturer) also does much of the design.
Whether a hardware maker can raise prices when parts get dearer. If it can't, its gross margin shrinks; if demand is strong, it may even widen.
Hard disk drives store data magnetically on spinning platters; solid-state drives use NAND flash chips. SSDs are faster, HDDs far cheaper per terabyte.
Nearline drives are high-capacity HDDs for cloud data centres. Drive makers track total capacity shipped in exabytes (a billion gigabytes) more than units.
Orders for AI servers that are booked but not yet shipped. It points to future revenue, but is tied to the customer's GPU supply and financing.
How many extra products or services are sold per device, such as storage, warranties or subscriptions.
Selling the device cheaply and earning the profit on supplies or services later, as with printers and ink.

drivers.name: Consumer spending and upgrade cycles
drivers.how: Phone and PC demand rises with household income and confidence, and with reasons to upgrade, such as a strong new iPhone, new AI features, or the end of support for an old version of Windows.

drivers.name: Memory and component costs
drivers.how: When DRAM and NAND prices jump, the parts bill rises. Device makers must raise prices, which cuts unit demand, or absorb the cost, which cuts margins. Storage makers can gain from the same shortage.

drivers.name: Data-centre and AI build-out
drivers.how: Cloud and AI spending lifts orders for servers and high-capacity drives. AI servers add a lot of revenue but at low margins, so profit grows more slowly than sales.

drivers.name: Corporate IT budgets
drivers.how: Businesses buy most PCs, servers and storage arrays. They delay purchases when profits are under pressure and catch up later.

drivers.name: Tariffs and where things are made
drivers.how: Most devices are assembled in China and other Asian countries. Tariffs and trade rules change costs, and moving production to India, Vietnam or Mexico is slow and expensive.

drivers.name: The dollar
drivers.how: Much revenue comes from outside the U.S., so a stronger dollar lowers reported revenue unless prices abroad are raised.

business: Most revenue is one-off device sales: phones, PCs, servers, storage drives and arrays, and printers. Recurring streams come from services attached to devices (Apple's Services revenue was a record $31.6 billion in one quarter [1]), printer ink and toner, warranties and support contracts, and storage subscriptions.

Consumers buy most phones, many PCs and printers, through carriers, retailers and online stores. Businesses and governments buy PCs, servers and storage, often through resellers. Cloud and AI companies are now the biggest buyers of servers and high-capacity drives [4][7].

Components dominate: cost of goods sold averaged 61.64% of sales for U.S. computer and peripheral firms in January 2026 [13], and memory and processors are the largest items. Then come contract assembly, logistics, tariffs, R&D at 7.08% of sales [13], and marketing.

Brand, ecosystem and technology. Apple's combination of hardware, software and services lets it charge premium prices, with a 47.9% gross margin [1], and the hard-drive duopoly has pricing power when supply is tight [6][7]. Makers of standard PCs, Android phones and servers have little, so they must pass on component costs or absorb them [5].

Assets are inventory, receivables from carriers and resellers, brands, patents and, for drive makers, factories. Many are asset-light because contract manufacturers own the assembly plants. Liabilities are mainly payables to suppliers, which fund working capital, and debt used for buybacks or acquisitions; Seagate repaid about $1.2 billion of debt in one quarter [6].

Mostly asset-light. Net capex was 2.90% of sales across U.S. computer and peripheral firms, and sales were 3.62 times invested capital, high turnover by any standard [16]. Drive makers, which run their own factories, are the more capital-intensive part.
overview: We found no sourced total market size for this sub-industry. Shipments give the scale: IDC counted 255.3 million smartphones and 62.7 million PCs in Q3 2026, each down about a fifth [3][2]. U.S. computer and peripheral firms grew revenue 6.71% a year over five years [18]: a mature industry with a fast-growing server niche.

Smartphones and tablets; PCs and workstations; servers, now split between traditional and AI servers; storage (hard drives, flash and storage systems); printers and imaging; and wearables and accessories. Smartphones are the largest by revenue, led by Apple, and AI servers are the fastest growing [1][4].

Hardware makers sit between component suppliers (chips, memory, displays, drives) and buyers. Most rely on contract manufacturers in Asia for assembly. Downstream they sell through carriers, retailers, distributors and resellers, or directly to large customers. Operating systems and apps from other sub-industries make the devices useful.

The industry grew from mainframes and minicomputers to PCs in the 1980s and 1990s, then to smartphones after 2007, which made Apple the dominant profit pool. PC and phone markets have matured, with long replacement cycles. Cloud computing moved server buying to a few big customers, and AI is now making servers the growth engine again [4].

Design and brands are concentrated in the U.S., China, South Korea and Taiwan. Assembly is concentrated in China, with growing shares in India, Vietnam and Mexico. Sales are global, and Chinese brands Xiaomi, OPPO and vivo rank third to fifth in smartphones worldwide [3].
competition: Few in each product. Smartphones and PCs each have about five global brands with most of the market; high-capacity hard drives effectively have two; servers have several big names plus Asian makers selling directly to cloud companies; printers have a handful [2][3][11].

Apple is the largest company here. Samsung (22.6%) and Apple (22.4%) lead smartphones [3]; Lenovo (23.8%), HP (16.5%) and Dell (12.1%) lead PCs [2]; Dell, Super Micro and Hewlett Packard Enterprise are big in servers [4]; Seagate and Western Digital dominate hard drives [11]; and HP leads printers.

Consolidated. Decades of exits and mergers (IBM sold its PC business to Lenovo, and Hitachi's drive business went to Western Digital) have left a few leaders in each product. The top five brands hold most of the PC and smartphone markets [2][3].

High at scale: brands, distribution, supplier relationships and the volume needed to win good component prices take years to build, and hard-drive technology needs deep engineering know-how [6]. Barriers are lower in assembling standard servers or PCs, which is why Asian makers compete there on price.

Important. Bigger makers buy components more cheaply, get priority in shortages, and spread R&D and marketing over more units. The 2026 memory squeeze shows it: IDC said smaller smartphone brands fell further than Samsung and Apple [3].

Mixed. Standard PCs, Android phones and servers are close to commodities with thin margins; HP's PC business earned 4.6% [5]. Apple's devices and high-capacity drives are differentiated and earn far more [1][6].

In 2026, suppliers: a few memory makers control a scarce input whose cost IDC says is up about 350% for phones [3]. Large buyers such as cloud companies have strong power over server makers, which in our view is one reason AI servers earn thin margins. Apple holds unusual power over its own suppliers because of its volume.
drivers: Replacement cycles, new features such as AI on devices, consumer and corporate budgets, and the data-centre build-out for servers and storage. Price and mix matter as much as units: Apple's revenue rose 12% in a quarter while global smartphone shipments fell 22% [1][3].

Component costs relative to selling prices, product mix between premium and entry-level, services and supplies revenue, and scale. The average pre-tax operating margin was 22.48% for U.S. computer and peripheral firms in January 2026 [13], an average lifted by Apple; PC makers earn single digits [5].
Memory (DRAM and NAND), processors, displays, contract assembly, freight, tariffs and currency. In 2026 memory is the dominant swing cost [3][8].

Moderate. Consumer devices are partly financed through carriers and credit, and corporate IT budgets react to the cost of capital, but most of these firms carry little debt relative to their market value [15]. The larger effect is indirect, through consumer spending and valuations.

Sensitive to employment and consumer confidence, because phones and PCs are purchases that can be delayed; IDC says a weaker economy could cut PC demand further [2]. Component inflation is the main commodity exposure. A strong dollar lowers reported sales, because much revenue is earned abroad.

Cyclical and mature for consumer devices, with secular growth in servers and data-centre storage. U.S. computer and peripheral firms grew revenue 6.71% a year over five years, against 12.77% for the market [18]. Apple's services add a steadier, more defensive element.
financials: Modest. Revenue grew 6.71% a year and net income 14.01% a year over the five years to January 2026 for U.S. computer and peripheral firms, and analysts expected 25.42% annual EPS growth over the next five years [18], driven by AI servers and storage.

The average gross margin was 38.36% and pre-tax operating margin 22.48% in January 2026 [13]. The spread is wide: Apple's gross margin was 47.9% [1], the drive makers' operating margins are near 50% [6][7], and HP's PC business earned 4.6% [5].

Damodaran's unadjusted ROE for the group is -0.17%, which we read as distorted by firms with tiny or negative book equity after years of buybacks; adjusted for R&D it is 48.43% [14]. Asset-light leaders such as Apple earn very high returns on the little capital they use, but we found no sourced sub-industry ROIC.

Low against market value: market debt is under 5% of capital [15]. Book debt is high relative to book capital, at 61.31% [15], because buybacks have shrunk equity. The drive makers carry more debt and are paying it down [6].

Generally strong, because capex is low and suppliers fund working capital. Seagate generated $1.48 billion of free cash flow in one quarter on $211 million of capex [6], and Western Digital $1.38 billion [7]. Apple returned $28 billion to shareholders in one quarter [1].

Low: net capex was 2.90% of sales, and capex was 119.84% of depreciation across the group [16]. Assembly is outsourced, so most capital goes into tooling, data centres for services and, at the drive makers, factories.

In January 2026 the group traded at a forward P/E of 36.15 [10] and at 25.42 times EV/EBITDA, against 19.73 times for the market [17]. Those averages are lifted by Apple and the storage rally, and single names vary widely: Seagate traded on a forward P/E of 25 in October [11].
risks: Tariffs and trade rules are the main lever, as recent tariff refunds at Apple and HP show [1][5]. Right-to-repair laws, app-store and competition rules (which touch Apple's services), e-waste and energy-efficiency standards, and privacy rules also matter.

AI features on phones and PCs could revive replacement cycles, and AI data centres drive demand for servers and storage. The risks are flash storage replacing hard drives in more uses, AI moving work to the cloud so that devices matter less, and new device types reshuffling the leaders.
Limited but real. Saturated markets in rich, ageing countries mean growth must come from replacement and premium upgrades, while younger emerging markets such as India still add many new users.

People keep phones and PCs longer, which lowers unit demand, but they are buying more premium devices and paying for services, which lifts revenue per user [1]. Printing continues a long decline as documents go digital.

Chinese brands compete on price in phones and PCs, Asian contract makers sell servers directly to cloud companies, and hyperscalers design their own servers. Subscription models, sometimes called hardware as a service, could change how businesses buy PCs.

The industry depends heavily on assembly in China and on chips and memory from Taiwan and South Korea. Tariffs, export controls and tensions around Taiwan could disrupt supply or raise costs. Shifting production to India and Vietnam is under way but slow.

Smartphones have already absorbed cameras, music players and many PC tasks. Cloud storage substitutes for local drives, and flash substitutes for hard drives in faster tiers. Smart glasses and other wearables could one day take over some phone use.

opportunities: AI servers and data-centre storage keep growing, with Dell's $95 billion AI server backlog and rising exabyte demand for drives [4][7].
AI features on devices could shorten replacement cycles after a weak 2026 for phones and PCs.
Services and other recurring revenue raise profit per device, led by Apple's record Services revenue [1].
threats: Memory shortages could keep squeezing device demand and margins into 2027 and beyond [3][8].
Tariffs and supply-chain disruption, especially around China and Taiwan, could raise costs [1].
AI servers earn thin margins, and storage pricing could reverse from today's peak [6][11].
horizon.assessment: This sub-industry is really two businesses. Consumer devices are mature, and over 3 to 5 years their growth depends on whether AI features revive upgrades and memory costs ease; IDC does not expect a smartphone recovery before 2028 [3]. Data-centre hardware is growing fast, but with thin margins in servers and cyclical pricing in storage. Apple's ecosystem and services make it the steadiest earner. Our view is that the biggest risk is assuming today's peak storage margins and AI server growth will last a full cycle.

paragraphs: This group is being driven less by the general economic cycle than by an input-cost shock. IDC says memory costs for smartphones have risen about 350% since last year, with sequential increases slowing to the low double digits in the third quarter from roughly 50-100% in earlier quarters [3]. For PCs, IDC says the economy has weakened since last quarter, which could reduce demand further through the rest of 2026 and into 2027 [2]. Pricing will stay well above year-ago levels, and channel concern about inventory could bring promotions in the near term [2]. Consumer-facing hardware therefore faces a squeeze: higher bills of materials meet softer household budgets.

Enterprise-facing hardware sits in a different part of the cycle. Dell's fiscal second quarter 2027 revenue rose 58% to $47.0 billion, with a $95 billion AI server backlog, as data-centre spending ran well ahead of the broader economy [4]. Trade policy is a second macro variable. Apple said tariff refunds added about one percentage point to its September-quarter gross margin and $0.05 to earnings per share [1], and HP's guidance includes $0.19 of tariff-refund benefit for fiscal 2026 [5]. Those are one-off gains, and we would not treat them as run-rate. I did not locate a current source on interest-rate or currency effects specific to this sub-industry, so I make no claim there.

Demand has split in two. Consumer devices are shrinking on price. IDC's preliminary data show third-quarter 2026 smartphone shipments fell 22.0% to 255.3 million units, the largest year-over-year decline IDC has recorded, and it expects growth to stay constrained through 2027 with recovery possibly not until 2028 [3]. Worldwide PC shipments fell 20.1% to 62.7 million units, as early-year pull-forward ahead of price rises and supply constraints removed the usual seasonal lift [2].

Infrastructure demand runs the other way. Dell booked $60.9 billion of AI server orders in one quarter and lifted its fiscal 2027 AI-optimized server revenue outlook to $74 billion from $60 billion [4]. In storage, Western Digital's chief financial officer attributed growth to robust exabyte growth and improved pricing [7], and Seagate guided fiscal second quarter revenue to $4.8 billion, plus or minus $100 million, against $4.2 billion in the quarter just reported [6]. Memory makers are shifting capacity toward AI servers, and TrendForce-sourced reporting says PC DRAM supply could fall in 2027 [8]. Our read is that AI data creation is a structural driver for storage and servers, while for phones and PCs the 2026 decline is mostly a cost-and-price effect that could ease if memory supply loosens. Shortage end-date forecasts vary by company, from 2028 to 2030 for some memory makers [8].

Concentration differs sharply by product. In PCs, IDC's third-quarter data show Lenovo with 23.8% share (14.9 million units), HP 16.5%, Dell 12.1%, Apple 9.5% and ASUS 8.7% [2]. In smartphones, Samsung (22.6%) and Apple (22.4%) lead, followed by Xiaomi (12.0%), OPPO (10.0%) and vivo (7.5%) [3]. Hard drives are described as a virtual duopoly between Seagate and Western Digital in high-capacity drives, though that source gives no share figures [11].

Applying Porter's five forces: supplier power has risen sharply because a handful of memory makers control a scarce input whose cost IDC says is up about 350% for phones [3]. Buyer power is high for PC and phone makers selling to price-sensitive consumers, but weaker for storage vendors, since Western Digital cites deeper customer relationships and expanding visibility into future demand [7]. Threat of substitutes is modest for devices, though cloud storage substitutes for local capacity in some uses. Threat of new entrants is low in hard drives and premium phones, given scale and technology barriers. Rivalry is intense in PCs and Android phones, where Xiaomi, OPPO and vivo saw deeper declines than Samsung and Apple [3]. Pricing power is therefore strongest at Apple, whose September-quarter gross margin was 47.9% [1], and at the storage duopoly, whose gross margins were 57.3% (Seagate, GAAP) [6] and 57.8% (Western Digital, GAAP) [7].

Policy risk is mainly trade. Apple reported tariff refunds that lifted its fiscal fourth quarter gross margin by about one percentage point [1], and HP's guidance includes tariff-refund benefits of $0.08 in its fiscal fourth quarter and $0.19 for the full fiscal 2026 year [5]. Both show tariffs have been a live cost and are now generating one-off reversals. I was unable to open a source on the current tariff status for computers and phones, so I do not characterise the forward tariff regime.

Technology is the other lever. HP said it is mitigating memory costs through pricing, redesigning some PCs and similar actions [5]. In storage, Seagate's chief executive tied its HAMR-based roadmap to meeting growing exabyte demand through areal density gains while maintaining supply discipline [6]. In servers, Dell's traditional servers and networking grew 122% and storage 26% in its latest quarter, showing AI is pulling through adjacent infrastructure [4]. Supply-chain concentration is an emerging risk: suppliers are moving capacity toward AI servers, and one report, unconfirmed by the companies, claims Samsung and SK hynix may cut PC DRAM output by 20% to 40% in 2027 [8]. Treat that as a rumour, not a fact.

Economics are diverging by sub-segment. Apple's September-quarter revenue was $114.5 billion, up 12%, with iPhone at $57.6 billion and Services at a record $31.6 billion; fiscal 2026 revenue was a record $478.8 billion [1]. At Dell, the infrastructure group earned a 15% operating margin against 8.8% a year earlier, while the client group earned $1.14 billion on $15.0 billion of revenue, roughly 7.6% by our arithmetic [4]. HP's Personal Systems margin was 4.6%, down from 5.4%, as higher commodity costs outweighed repricing [5].

Storage vendors are the most profitable. Seagate posted $4.23 billion of revenue, a 57.8% non-GAAP gross margin, a 50.7% non-GAAP operating margin and $1.48 billion of free cash flow in a quarter with only $211 million of capital expenditure [6]. Western Digital reported $4.38 billion of revenue, a 49.1% non-GAAP operating margin and $1.38 billion of free cash flow [7]. Capital intensity is therefore low relative to profit at the drive makers, and operating leverage on price has been large. Super Micro's fiscal fourth quarter adjusted EPS was $1.70 against a $0.92 analyst forecast, although I could not retrieve its margin or revenue from an opened page [12]. I did not find sub-industry ROIC or ROE from a source I opened.

Guidance is strong at the infrastructure and storage end. Dell guided fiscal 2027 revenue to $192 billion, up 69%, and non-GAAP EPS to $25.50, up 148%; for the third quarter it guided revenue to about $49 billion and non-GAAP EPS to $6.50 [4]. Seagate guided fiscal second quarter non-GAAP EPS to $9.20, plus or minus $0.20 [6]; Western Digital guided revenue to $5.1 billion, gross margin to 60%-61% and EPS to $5.80 [7]. HP raised fiscal 2026 adjusted EPS guidance to $3.19-$3.29 including tariff refunds, and expects PC units to fall in the high teens in the second half [5]. Apple gave no forward guidance in its release [1].

For context on the market, FactSet reports blended third-quarter S&P 500 earnings growth of 30.2% as of 30 October 2026 and names Information Technology among the sectors with double-digit growth, though it did not give the sector figure in the text I opened [9]. I could not obtain consensus estimates for this sub-industry. Our view is that unit declines of around 20% in phones and PCs [2][3] make consumer-hardware earnings dependent on pricing and mix, so consensus for those names carries more risk than for storage, where guidance already embeds sharply higher pricing. That is judgment, not a sourced estimate.

The most recent sub-industry multiple I could open is dated. Damodaran's January 2026 US dataset for Computers/Peripherals (36 firms) shows a trailing P/E of 81.13, a forward P/E of 36.15 and a PEG ratio of 1.35 [10]. These predate the large price moves since, so I treat them as a historical reference, not a current reading. For the broad market, FactSet put the S&P 500 forward 12-month P/E at 18.7 on 30 October 2026, below the five-year average of 19.8 and the 10-year average of 19.1 [9]. I did not find a current Information Technology sector forward multiple.

Single-name data show wide dispersion. A Motley Fool article lists Seagate at a forward P/E of 25 and Western Digital at 23, with five-year PEG ratios of 0.53 and 0.90 respectively [11]. Those multiples sit on guidance of very high earnings growth, for example Seagate's guided EPS of $9.20 against $7.68 in the prior quarter [6]. Our read is that storage is priced for the memory and exabyte upcycle to persist, and the risk is a normalisation of pricing, while consumer-device names must be judged on whether memory costs can be passed through [2][5]. I did not obtain free-cash-flow yields.

Price momentum is concentrated in storage. A Motley Fool article reports Seagate up 235% year to date and 292% over 12 months, and Western Digital up 164% and 278%; its quote data show both shares falling sharply on 5 November 2026, with Seagate down 16.25% to $466.53 and Western Digital down 17.36% to $267.63 [11]. Whether that reflects earnings reactions or a broader rotation is not stated in the source, and I have not verified the cause.

The fundamental backdrop for those moves is the pricing cycle: DRAM contract prices hit a record in October 2026 while the 128Gb MLC NAND price held flat after 21 months of increases, a pause that may reflect inventory adjustment rather than a turn [8]. Western Digital raised its dividend 17% to $0.175 per share [7], and Seagate repaid about $1.2 billion of debt in the quarter [6], so balance sheets are being repaired while shares trade at high multiples to earnings growth. Apple returned $28 billion in the September quarter [1]. I did not find ETF flow, short-interest or breadth data for this sub-industry from a source I opened, so I do not characterise institutional positioning.
